I have been working in a small SaaS company as a senior software engineer for the last few years as an independent contributor

Since the last 6 months, my colleagues have gone completely crazy about the AI craze. Initially, they were doing whole work through AI.

Now they have outsourced communication to AI too. If I ask a question to a colleague, I will get a 500-word paragraph generated by AI with actual information hidden deep somewhere, sometimes even missing.

QA guy who doesn't know how to program has become very opinionated and argumentative about software coding. When he report a bug, instead of 2-4 lines, he create a ticket with 200 lines of blah blah blah

Team lead is pro AI. While she uses her own word to communicate, she doesn't discourage other from speaking in AI.

How do I discourage others from outsourcing communication to AI and talk like humans again?

I manage a small team of data analysts at a medium-sized public services company in the UK.

I have a colleague, whom I'll call Mark. Mark is, for the most part, conscientious and professional, but he has a particular habit which I find very frustrating: he asks for multiple rounds of revisions, often very minor ones, after we've delivered what he initially requested. Extra data fields added, reworked graphs, slight variations on filtering, that sort of thing. He does this with whoever is assigned to the task, not just me, and I've been told it's the same when he's working with people elsewhere in the business.

I know it's not always possible to anticipate exactly what you need right from the outset, but I genuinely believe Mark could better prepare himself for at least some of these "extra" requirements before handing us the initial brief. How can I reduce the impact this practice has on me and my direct reports?

A few things I've tried:

  • Talking to Mark: We've had the conversation a few times. Sometimes he tries to make a joke out of it, but I do genuinely believe he understands the problem in the abstract and is sympathetic; it just doesn't seem to translate well to action.

  • Refining the brief: Where possible, we will always have a quick discussion or Teams call with Mark to iron out exactly what's needed, often bringing up things which we think he's likely to ask for later. This does seem to help at least a little, but, when we think we're done, there's still always "just one more thing".

  • Building self-service tools: Mark has expressed an interest in being able to do some of his own data processing and analysis. He has the technical chops, but we can't get him direct database access for silly IT reasons (beyond the scope of this post!), and his needs are too variable to be served by a Power BI dashboard or similar.

  • Just saying no: Mark moves between major projects every few months, but they usually have a very senior sponsor who will push the revisions through as a priority. It's always a legitimate business need, too - in my judgement, the revisions Mark asks for are very rarely frivolous or "just in case" - so it's difficult to reject.
